claims.text: Edge dislocations control high-temperature strength and strength retention in BCC NbTaTiV and CrMoNbV refractory high-entropy alloys.
Edge-dislocation-mediated deformation is atypical relative to the screw-dislocation-controlled plastic flow generally found in elemental BCC metals and dilute alloys.
Intrinsic lattice distortion reinforces the dominance of edge-dislocation-mediated deformation in refractory HEAs.
Short-range chemical ordering reinforces edge-dislocation-mediated deformation.
The edge-dislocation mechanism produces stable thermoelastic behavior at high temperature.
Oxygen and nitrogen interstitials promote phase segregation during thermal aging of Ti-V-Nb-Ta refractory HEAs.
Interstitial-induced phase segregation depletes strengthening interstitial solutes from the matrix and causes progressive age softening.
Controlled oxygen or nitrogen additions will promote phase segregation relative to an otherwise identical ultra-pure alloy during high-temperature exposure.
Edge-dislocation networks coupled with short-range chemical order increase lattice friction and restrict dislocation mobility at high temperatures.
Severe multicomponent lattice distortion causes edge-dislocation propagation to be favored over conventional screw-dislocation pathways.
Interstitial impurities disrupt local chemical order.
Interstitial-driven phase segregation causes a transition in dislocation behavior.
Ultra-pure samples will retain greater high-temperature yield strength than impurity-doped samples after thermal exposure.
Ultra-pure samples will exhibit stable elastic moduli, whereas impurity-doped samples will exhibit an altered thermoelastic response.
The proposed mechanism primarily applies to single-phase BCC refractory HEAs at high temperature.
Refractory alloys with substantial multiphase character or high fractions of HCP elements may operate through different deformation mechanisms.
